interactionPlan.concept: A random-dot stereogram encodes a hidden depth-defined shape through binocular disparity, even though each single-eye dot field looks like unstructured noise.
elements: left random-dot field: a dense rectangular black-and-white dot panel with no border or label in the default view
right random-dot field: a dense rectangular black-and-white dot panel with no border or label in the default view
narrow central white separation between the two dot panels
shared deterministic random-dot background pattern used to generate corresponding dots in both panels
central hidden square disparity region whose dots are horizontally shifted between the left and right panels but has no visible outline in the raw view
optional reveal overlay: thin colored square outline marking the hidden disparity region
optional reveal overlay: small horizontal displacement arrows inside or near the central square
optional reveal overlay: concise label 'shifted dot region' placed outside the dot fields

interactions.label: Overlay
interactions.teaches: The hidden square is not drawn as a normal outline in either image; it is recoverable only by comparing corresponding dot shifts between the two eye images

demo_steps.title: Raw stereogram
demo_steps.narration: The default view is only two dense black-and-white random-dot fields separated by a central gap. With one eye image alone, no square should be explicitly outlined or labeled.

demo_steps.title: Reveal the encoded disparity
demo_steps.narration: Turning on the optional overlay marks the square-shaped region where corresponding dots are shifted between the two panels. The overlay explains the construction but is not part of the original stereogram.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The shape is invisible as a monocular picture but appears in depth when the visual system matches the two shifted dot patterns.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Prioritize visual fidelity to the source: the default rendered state should be almost entirely occupied by two side-by-side dense black-and-white random-dot rectangles with a clean central white separation, no axes, no panel borders, no titles, no explanatory arrows, and no square outline. Use a seeded deterministic dot pattern so the SVG is reproducible; render many small high-contrast black and white square or circular dot marks with visible fill, similar density and scale across both panels. The two panels should share the same underlying random-dot field except for a centered square patch whose dot coordinates are horizontally displaced between left and right images. Keep UI minimal and away from the dot panels; the single overlay toggle should be secondary. In reveal mode only, draw a thin translucent colored square outline and small arrows showing the horizontal disparity, without changing the underlying dot fields.

plan.concept: A random dot stereogram shows that the visual system can perceive a floating or recessed shape from binocular disparity alone, even when neither eye's image contains a recognizable object by itself.
elements: left-eye random dot image panel with black and white dots
right-eye random dot image panel with black and white dots
matching random dot background shared between the two panels
central square region whose dot pattern is horizontally displaced between the two panels
label 'Left eye image' above the left panel
label 'Right eye image' above the right panel
subtle panel border around each random dot image
optional fixation marks centered above or between the panels
disparity reveal overlay outlining the hidden central square
horizontal arrows showing the left-right displacement of the square region when reveal mode is active
annotation text explaining 'same dots, shifted square region'
depth cue label indicating 'appears in front' for one disparity sign and 'appears behind' for the opposite sign

interactions.label: Square disparity
interactions.teaches: The magnitude and sign of the horizontal displacement between the two eye images determine how far the hidden square appears from the background and whether it appears in front of or behind it

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: The square is not defined by recognizable monocular features; it becomes visible only when the two images are compared for relative displacement

demo_steps.title: No monocular object
demo_steps.narration: In the raw stereogram, each eye sees only random black and white dots. Looking at either panel alone gives no obvious square or shape cue.

demo_steps.title: Reveal the hidden displacement
demo_steps.narration: Switching to the revealed view outlines the central square and shows that its dots are shifted horizontally between the two panels. The shape exists as a disparity pattern, not as a visible outline in either image.

demo_steps.title: Change perceived depth
demo_steps.narration: Increasing the disparity makes the square appear separated farther in depth from the flat background. Reversing the sign changes whether the square is perceived as floating in front or lying behind.

demo_steps.title: Try fusion
demo_steps.narration: Return to the raw stereogram and try free fusion or a stereoscope. If each eye receives the correct panel, the visual system detects the disparity and the hidden square pops out in depth.

plan.keyInsight: Depth can be computed from relative displacement between the two eye images even when the images contain no recognizable monocular shape cues.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Create two large side-by-side rectangular panels filled with high-contrast black and white random dots. Use the same underlying dot pattern in both panels, but within a centered square patch shift the dots horizontally by the slider-controlled disparity amount between the left and right images. In raw mode, do not draw a square outline; the central square should be invisible or nearly invisible when either panel is viewed alone. In revealed mode, add a translucent colored square outline over the displaced region and small horizontal arrows indicating the disparity direction. Keep the figure visually sparse outside the dot fields so attention stays on the fact that the square is encoded only by binocular disparity.
